content.title: About
content.content: Chili with chicken is a spicy dish where bite‑size pieces of chicken breast are simmered in a sauce made from tomatoes, beans, chili peppers, and aromatic spices. The dish is popular in American, Mexican, and South American cuisines, offering protein, fiber, and moderate fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally chili is cooked in large pots, allowing flavors to meld over time.
There are many variations: beef, turkey, bean‑only, and vegetarian versions.
Chili peppers contain capsaicin, which provides heat and may boost metabolism.
The dish is often served with rice, corn tortillas, or guacamole.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The recipe supplies vitamins B6 and B12, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Beans and vegetables add dietary fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Tomatoes and chili peppers are rich in lycopene and vitamin C, which protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Moderate fat content
items.content: When prepared with minimal added oil, chili with chicken remains low in saturated fats.

items.title: Spiciness
items.content: Capsaicin can cause stomach irritation in people with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Using ready‑made broths or sauces can raise salt levels; adjust seasoning accordingly.

items.title: Beans and gas
items.content: Legumes may cause bloating for some; soaking beans before cooking can reduce this effect.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot chili with chicken over steamed rice, with corn tortillas, a dollop of sour cream, or shredded cheese. Fresh cilantro, lime wedges, or guacamole add brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the dish to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

coffee-cafe-mocha-decaffeinated-with-non.title: Coffee, Cafe Mocha, Decaffeinated, with Non‑Dairy Milk

content.title: About
content.content: Cafe Mocha is a fragrant beverage made from espresso, chocolate syrup, and non‑dairy milk (soy, almond, or oat). The decaffeinated version retains the characteristic flavor without the stimulating effect. It is popular in cafés as a sweet, creamy treat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mocha is named after the Yemeni port of Mocha, historically a coffee trade hub.
Chocolate syrup is often crafted from cocoa mass, sugar, and vanilla, giving the drink a deep aroma.
Decaffeinated espresso is produced by removing caffeine from green beans, usually with water or CO₂ methods.
Non‑dairy milks are made from nuts, beans, or grains and are fortified with vitamins, suitable for vegetarians and vegans.
Cafe Mocha is frequently topped with plant‑based whipped cream and a dusting of cocoa powder.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Chocolate syrup contains flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Mood support
items.content: Even without caffeine, the aromatic profile of espresso can uplift mood through olfactory pathways.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Plant milks are often enriched with calcium, vitamin D, and B12, supporting bone and nervous system health.

items.title: Moderate sugar content
items.content: Using unsweetened plant milk and a controlled amount of syrup keeps the drink moderately sweet without excess sugar.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Some plant milks, such as oat milk, contain beta‑glucans that promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Allergy to plant ingredients
items.content: Individuals may be allergic to soy, almond, or oat milk.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Chocolate syrup adds sugar; people monitoring glucose levels should watch portion size.

items.title: Possible additives
items.content: Some commercial syrups may contain artificial flavors and preservatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, topped with plant‑based whipped cream and a sprinkle of cocoa powder. A pinch of cinnamon or a dash of vanilla extract can add variety.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The prepared drink is best enjoyed immediately. If stored, keep it in a sealed container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours. Store plant milk according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

content.title: About
content.content: White cooked rice (NS) is a processed grain from which the outer layers (bran and germ) have been removed. After cooking it becomes soft, slightly sticky, and has a neutral flavor, making it a versatile base for many dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rice is a staple food for more than half of the world’s population.
White rice has a longer shelf life than whole‑grain rice because the oily germ has been removed.
In Japan rice is often used for sushi‑rice, which is seasoned with vinegar, sugar, and salt after cooking.
In China rice is traditionally served as “congee,” where the grains stay separate and fluffy.
Rice can be grown in flooded paddies, which helps control weeds.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: White rice is rich in carbohydrates that quickly convert to glucose, providing a rapid energy boost.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The lack of bran makes cooked white rice gentle on the digestive tract, suitable for diets after gastrointestinal upset.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: A 100 g serving of cooked rice contains less than 0.5 g of fat, fitting low‑fat eating plans.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice provides thiamine (B1), niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which are involved in carbohydrate metabolism.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Magnesium, phosphorus and iron in rice support muscle function and blood health.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Low fiber content
items.content: The removal of bran makes rice less beneficial for digestion compared with whole‑grain cereals.

items.title: Arsenic presence
items.content: In some regions rice may contain trace arsenic; rinsing the rice before cooking is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rice can be served as a side dish with meat, fish, or vegetables, used in soups, pilafs, sushi, rice salads, or as a base for risotto. For added flavor, cook rice in broth or add herbs and spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice should be cooled quickly and kept in the refrigerator for no more than 3‑4 days, or frozen for longer storage.
